report.source_text: A lumbar puncture was performed including analyses of cell count, protein, lactate and glucose as well as a broad microbiological assay since the patient was under immunomodulating treatment. White (<0,003×109/L) and red (<0,0003×1012/L) cell count, glucose (3.6 mmol/L), lactate (1.8 mmol/L) and albumin (155 mg/L) were normal. CSF was positive for VZV-DNA. In serum, VZV IgG was positive, and IgM was at the threshold limit value.

report.source_text: Treatment with natalizumab was paused. The patient was asymptomatic during in-hospital stay and discharged home after 7 days. Acyclovir was administered intravenously until the follow-up lumbar puncture, when VZV-PCR DNA was negative. Virological and microbiological analyses as above were still negative. clinician.trajectory_summary: A woman in her 30s with relapsing-remitting MS and a history of recent right-sided ophthalmic zoster presented with new onset headache, photophobia, phonophobia, and recurrent right cheek twitches. Brain MRI revealed subacute ischemic changes in the right basal ganglia and right cerebral peduncle, along with narrowing and gadolinium enhancement of the supraclinoid segment of the right internal carotid artery (ICA) and the A1 segment of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA). Lumbar puncture showed normal CSF cell counts, protein, lactate, and albumin, but was positive for VZV-DNA. Based on these findings, cerebral zoster vasculopathy was diagnosed. Treatment was initiated with intravenous methylprednisolone, intravenous acyclovir, and acetylsalicylic acid. The patient became asymptomatic during her hospital stay and was discharged after 7 days. Natalizumab treatment was paused. A follow-up lumbar puncture showed negative VZV-PCR DNA. A follow-up MRI 6 weeks after the initial MRI showed persisting vasculitic vessel wall changes and gadolinium enhancement in the right ICA and ACA. Natalizumab treatment was terminated, and rituximab was started. A subsequent follow-up MRI 9 months later demonstrated regression of gadolinium enhancement in the vessel walls but persisting vessel wall thickening in the affected segments, with no new lesions.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with new onset headache and focal neurological symptoms (right cheek twitches) following a recent ophthalmic zoster infection.

Brain MRI demonstrated subacute ischemic changes in the right basal ganglia and cerebral peduncle, along with narrowing and gadolinium enhancement of the right ICA and ACA, consistent with vasculopathy.
CSF analysis was positive for VZV-DNA, confirming a viral etiology for the vasculopathy.
Clinical improvement (asymptomatic) and clearance of VZV-DNA from CSF followed treatment with antiviral and anti-inflammatory medications.
Follow-up brain MRI showed regression of active inflammation (gadolinium enhancement) but persistent vessel wall thickening, indicating resolution of acute vasculitis.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: The MRI findings of vessel wall enhancement and narrowing, along with positive VZV-DNA in CSF, are not typical for an MS relapse and strongly point to an infectious vasculopathy.
The detection of VZV-DNA in the CSF specifically identifies VZV as the causative agent of the vasculitis.

remaining_uncertainties: Long-term clinical outcome beyond 9 months post-diagnosis.
Specific duration of antiviral and antiplatelet therapy.
Long-term efficacy of rituximab in this specific context.
